comment: The design principles are architectural properties and do not include a principle about the unit of obligation. The difference between obliging an exchange between two named parties and obliging a state of affairs - that a datum be findable and interpretable where there is a lawful basis - is architecturally consequential: the first requires a bilateral relationship per pair and scales quadratically, the second requires a shared capability and scales linearly.

public.text: The design principles are architectural properties and do not include a principle about the unit of obligation. The difference between obliging an exchange between two named parties and obliging a state of affairs - that a datum be findable and interpretable where there is a lawful basis - is architecturally consequential: the first requires a bilateral relationship per pair and scales quadratically, the second requires a shared capability and scales linearly.
public.suggestedRevision: Add a design principle on the unit of obligation: requirements should attach to the availability of information rather than to transfers between named parties. The consequences are that the number of relationships to be maintained changes from quadratic to linear, as section 1.3.1 already argues on cost grounds; the object of enforcement becomes a verifiable state rather than a message format; and responsibility for the whole becomes assignable to a holder. This is the core of the shift Dutch policy calls 'databeschikbaarheid'.
